notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on non-party access to pleadings and written openings after settlement.

enrichment.short_title: Non-party access to fraud allegations in settled film finance litigation
key_facts: HIH, not a party to the settled Hollywood 4 and 5 film finance proceedings, sought access to pleadings and written opening submissions relating to fraud allegations against JLT and Flashpoint.
Lexington's written opening contained wider unpleaded fraud allegations against JLT in respect of Hollywood 1 and 2; JLT's counsel objected before the case settled after five days of trial.
HIH wanted the material to consider similar fraud claims against JLT in related Hollywood 1-3 reinsurance proceedings.
Written openings were not court records and CPR 5.4(2)(c) did not apply to them; CPR 31.22 and CPR 32.13 were also inapplicable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in settled Commercial Court proceedings for disclosure of pleadings and written opening submissions to a non-party.
enrichment.outcome: HIH granted access to pleadings and written openings except passages alleging fraud against JLT in relation to Hollywood 1 and 2.
enrichment.ratio: Access to written opening submissions depends on the inherent jurisdiction and open justice; where a trial has commenced and the judge has read submissions deployed in conducting the hearing, a non-party may prima facie be entitled to them, but unpleaded allegations whose admissibility remained unresolved and which JLT had objected to opening should not be exposed to a non-party.
legal_issues: Whether non-party access could be ordered under CPR 5.4(2), CPR 31.22, CPR 32.13 or the inherent jurisdiction
Whether written openings formed part of the court record
Whether access should be refused where unpleaded fraud allegations had not been ruled admissible
How Gio and SmithKline Beecham apply where a case settles before judgment

notes: Complete rolled-up judicial review of a post-conviction anti-social behaviour order imposed by a youth court.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court section 1C ASBO quashed for procedural unfairness
key_facts: A 15-year-old with a substantial criminal record was sentenced on 12 June 2003 for escape from lawful custody and resisting a police officer.
On 8 May 2003 the same youth court had declined to impose an order under section 1C despite full prosecution submissions.
On 12 June the magistrates imposed a two-year order prohibiting any behaviour causing harassment, alarm or distress anywhere, without adequate reasons or procedural fairness.
The order was served on the wrong statutory form referring to section 1 rather than section 1C, and a wing magistrate appears to have supplied undisclosed information in deliberations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited rolled-up hearing for permission and substantive judicial review of a Sunderland Youth Court order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and substantive claim allowed; the section 1C order was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Although section 1C gives magistrates a broad discretion to make an order on conviction without a prior application, they must act fairly and reasonably; changing course within weeks without explanation, using the wrong form, and relying on undisclosed material renders the process unlawful even where statutory conditions were arguably met.
legal_issues: Whether orders under section 1C are civil or criminal for evidential purposes
What procedural fairness requires where the court proposes to make a section 1C order of its own motion
Whether magistrates could properly impose an order after refusing one on substantially the same history
Whether the order was impermissibly wide in geographical scope

notes: Complete preliminary judicial review on Newham homelessness allocation practice and UTCCR scope.

enrichment.short_title: Newham unlawful 'sign now or lose B&B' homelessness allocation policy

statutes_considered.title: Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: Three homeless households in Newham bed-and-breakfast were told to attend appointments, sign private sector leasing tenancies without viewing, and accept immediately or lose accommodation.
Khatun signed sight unseen and was placed above a public house; Zeb and Iqbal refused to sign without viewing and had their section 193 duties terminated.
Newham adopted the practice to meet government targets to move families out of bed-and-breakfast by April 2004.
The Office of Fair Trading intervened on whether the 1999 Regulations and Directive applied to local authority leases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Newham's allocation policy and preliminary issues on the scope of the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999.
enrichment.outcome: Claims allowed; the allocation policy was held unlawful and the Directive and 1999 Regulations were held to apply to land leases and to public authority landlords.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may not coerce homeless applicants into signing tenancy agreements without a reasonable opportunity to consider and, where requested, view accommodation, especially where statutory guidance requires that opportunity; the Unfair Terms Directive and Regulations apply to contracts transferring interests in land and to local housing authorities acting as suppliers.
legal_issues: Whether Newham's sign-on-the-spot policy was lawful under Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 and statutory guidance
Whether the policy was oppressive and departed from paragraph 9.12 of the Code of Guidance
Whether the 1999 Regulations and Directive 93/13/EEC apply to leases of land
Whether a local housing authority is a seller or supplier and a homeless tenant a consumer

notes: Complete judicial review quashing an Exceptional Circumstances Panel decision on housing transfer priority.

enrichment.short_title: Housing transfer panel could not exclude tenant after successful homelessness decision
key_facts: Mrs Bilverstone, a secure tenant who fled domestic violence at her Oxford council home, sought urgent transfer through the Exceptional Circumstances Panel.
Oxford City Council initially refused to refer her case for lack of corroborative evidence, then served notice to quit after she pursued a Part VII homelessness application.
On 12 March 2003 the Council accepted she was unintentionally homeless and in priority need; the next day the ECP refused transfer priority because she had succeeded under Part VII.
She remained in poor temporary Part VII accommodation while waiting for a permanent council tenancy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second judicial review challenge to Oxford City Council's Exceptional Circumstances Panel decision.
enrichment.outcome: ECP decision quashed; the panel must reconsider Mrs Bilverstone's case lawfully.
enrichment.ratio: Parts VI and VII of the Housing Act 1996 are not separate territories and a successful homelessness decision does not preclude separate consideration for transfer priority; nor did the tenant make a binding election between routes, and the Council's earlier delay could not be used against her.
legal_issues: Whether acceptance as statutorily homeless precluded Exceptional Circumstances Panel prioritisation
Whether the tenant had been put to an election between Part VI transfer and Part VII homelessness routes
Whether loss of secure tenancy status or service of notice to quit barred ECP consideration
Whether the Council's earlier failure to refer the case affected the lawfulness of the later decision

notes: Complete preliminary issue trial on construction of a reinsurance claims co-operation clause.

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurers' claims co-operation clause held not a condition precedent
key_facts: Eagle Star sought indemnity from reinsurers for settlement and defence costs arising from environmental claims against Varian Associates under a 1969-1970 liability policy.
Reinsurers argued clause (b) of the Claims Co-operation Clause made their control of negotiation and settlement a condition precedent to liability.
It was agreed reinsurers did not control the Varian settlement and Eagle Star paid US$1 million plus substantial defence costs.
The policy contained both a follow-the-settlements clause and an apportionment of costs clause requiring reinsurers' consent for legal costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on agreed facts in Commercial Court reinsurance proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Clause (b) was not a condition precedent; reinsurers could elect to take control, but if they did not, Eagle Star could settle and reinsurers would follow subject to other policy terms.
enrichment.ratio: Subparagraph (b) of a claims co-operation clause gives reinsurers an optional right to take control of negotiations and settlement; only if they exercise that control and the reinsured settles behind their backs are they relieved of liability, and clear words are required before such a clause is treated as a condition precedent.
legal_issues: Whether clause (b) imposed a positive obligation on the reinsured or a right exercisable by reinsurers
Whether clause (b) was a condition precedent to reinsurers' liability
How the claims co-operation clause interacted with the follow-the-settlements and apportionment of costs clauses
Whether the insolvency-clause reinsuring provision displaced the printed follow-the-settlements obligation

notes: Substantive appeal on Article 2 questions 1-4 allowed, but question 5 on funding powers was adjourned for further hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Hospital death inquest must allow effective family participation under Article 2
key_facts: Three-year-old Naazish Khan died at St James's Hospital, Leeds in October 1999 after a catastrophic potassium overdose during dialysis; gross negligence was alleged and the family feared a cover-up.
Police investigated, exhumed the body, and the CPS decided not to prosecute; NHS Trust investigations excluded the family entirely.
An inquest was adjourned while Mr Khan sought public funding for legal representation; the Secretary of State refused funding and a separate inquiry.
The Trust later admitted liability, but the family remained unable to participate effectively in the inquest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Silber J in judicial review proceedings against the Secretary of State for Health.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: declarations that the United Kingdom had not yet fulfilled its Article 2 obligations, that an inquest without effective family participation would not suffice, and that the Human Rights Act 1998 applied; further hearing ordered on the state's power to fund representation.
enrichment.ratio: Where a hospital death raises allegations of gross negligence and possible concealment, Article 2 requires an effective public investigation in which the deceased's family are involved to the extent necessary to safeguard their interests; that obligation remained unfulfilled here and could not be satisfied by prior police and internal NHS inquiries from which the family were excluded.
legal_issues: The content of the state's Article 2 procedural obligation in clinical negligence deaths
Whether police and NHS investigations had already discharged that obligation
Whether a coroner's inquest could suffice if the family could not participate effectively
Whether Article 2 rights were enforceable under the Human Rights Act 1998 where death occurred before October 2000
Whether the Secretary of State had power to fund legal representation at the inquest

notes: Complete judicial review dismissing an Article 8 challenge to Dublin Convention removal certification.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 certification upheld for Dublin return of Somali asylum seeker

statutes_considered.title: Convention determining the State responsible for examining applications for asylum lodged in one of the Member States of the European Communities (Dublin Convention)

key_facts: Abdullah Hussein, a Somali national, claimed asylum in the Netherlands as Mohamed Abdulla Gedi in 2000; his appeal failed but he remained in the Netherlands before entering the UK in April 2002 under a different name and date of birth.
He formed a relationship with Kifaaya Adan Yuusuf, whom he married in June 2002 and again in a civil ceremony in May 2003; she was granted humanitarian leave to remain.
The Netherlands accepted responsibility under the Dublin Convention and the Secretary of State certified his Article 8 claim as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a).
Hussein argued removal to the Netherlands would cause destitution and prolonged separation, and that exceptional family-link discretion should apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of certification under section 72(2)(a) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 following permission granted by Silber J.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the section 72 certification was upheld and the interim injunction lapsed.
enrichment.ratio: Following Ekinci, a claimant removed to a safe third country may be required to apply for entry clearance from there rather than avoid the entry-clearance system; absent exceptional circumstances, temporary separation and reliance on a capacitated spouse's emotional support do not make an Article 8 claim arguably well-founded where Dublin responsibility lies elsewhere.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant's marriage and dependency made his Article 8 claim arguable
Whether return to the Netherlands would expose him to Article 3-level destitution
Whether paragraph 2(f) of the family links policy applied
How Ekinci affects certification where entry clearance can later be sought from the third country

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on 1976 Limitation Convention fund jurisdiction and Singapore security.

enrichment.short_title: 1976 limitation fund valid in London but Singapore LOU not releasable under Article 13

statutes_considered.title: Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims 1976

key_facts: ICL VIKRAMAN sank after a collision in the Malacca Strait; cargo interests arrested a sister ship in Singapore and obtained a Club letter of undertaking approved by the Singapore High Court.
London arbitration produced a substantial cargo award, but ICL then constituted a 1976 Convention limitation fund in England.
ICL sought release of the LOU under Article 13(2); Chin Tai argued Singapore security was outside the Convention because Singapore was not a State Party.
The LOU covered sums due in the Singapore in rem action, London arbitration, or by agreement, up to US$4.5 million.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to set aside service of a limitation claim form and discharge an injunction, and for release of security under Article 13(2) of the 1976 Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Limitation fund validly constituted in England and service on Chin Tai upheld, but Article 13(2) did not require release of the Singapore LOU; the injunction restraining demand on the LOU could not stand on that basis.
enrichment.ratio: Article 11 permits constitution of a limitation fund where legal proceedings include London arbitration, and Article 13(2) operates only in respect of arrest or security within a State Party; security deployed to obtain release of a vessel in Singapore proceedings remains within Singapore jurisdiction and is not releasable by the English court under the 1976 Convention.
legal_issues: Whether London cargo arbitration counted as legal proceedings for Article 11.1
Whether CPR 61.11(5)(c) conferred jurisdiction to serve a limitation claim out of the jurisdiction
Whether Article 13(2) applied to a letter of undertaking given in Singapore proceedings
Where security is located for Article 13.2 purposes
Whether a limitation fund is actually available under Article 13.3 before a limitation decree

notes: Complete section 288 planning appeal challenge dismissed with immaterial policy omission.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt garage conversion appeal dismissed despite missing local plan paragraph
key_facts: Mr Burgess appealed against Guildford Borough Council's refusal of alterations to a dormer window, garage roof, external staircase and balcony at Ringwood Cottage in Holmbury St Mary.
The site was in the Green Belt, an AONB, an AGLV and a conservation area; the inspector dismissed the appeal as inappropriate harmful development.
Paragraph 5.41 of the local plan deposit version, explaining that detached garages could fall within Policy 99H9, was omitted from the inspector's papers.
The claimant argued the inspector misread Policy 12RE and made factual errors about visibility from woodland and overlooking of neighbouring property Heathcote.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's appeal decision following written representations and a site visit.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; relief withheld because any policy misreading was immaterial to the inspector's conclusions.
enrichment.ratio: Even if an inspector misunderstood that Policy 99H9 could in principle apply to extensions of detached outbuildings, relief should be withheld under Simplex where the inspector's detailed findings on harm to the Green Belt and landscape meant the proposal would inevitably have failed the policy criteria.
legal_issues: Whether omission of local plan paragraph 5.41 caused material misunderstanding of Policies 99H9 and 99RE2
Whether Policy 12RE was mischaracterised as imposing a presumption against all development
Whether the inspector irrationally described a landing as a balcony
Whether site-visit findings on visibility and privacy were perverse

notes: Complete reserved judgment on forced psychiatric medication of a capacitated detained patient.

enrichment.short_title: Capacitated detained patient refused injunction against compulsory anti-psychotics
key_facts: PS, a patient detained under section 37, had capacity to refuse anti-psychotic medication but his RMO and SOAD certified under section 58(3)(b) that treatment should be given.
There was a dispute between the responsible clinicians and the claimant's expert over diagnosis and treatability.
The claimant sought to prevent non-consensual medication, arguing that his capacitated refusal should prevail and that Articles 3, 8 and 14 ECHR would be breached.
The contested SOAD certificate was out of date by the time of the hearing, and a Mental Health Review Tribunal hearing was imminent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review with permission granted by Wall J to challenge RMO and SOAD decisions on proposed compulsory treatment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no breach of Articles 3, 8 or 14 was established and section 58 permitted the certified treatment despite the claimant's capacitated refusal.
enrichment.ratio: Section 58(3) permits compulsory treatment of a detained patient who refuses consent where a SOAD certifies that, having regard to alleviation or prevention of deterioration, treatment is appropriate; capacitated refusal does not automatically trump the statutory scheme, and proposed anti-psychotic treatment did not breach Articles 3 or 8 where it was necessary and proportionate for health protection.
legal_issues: Whether capacitated refusal to consent overrides section 58 certification
Whether proposed anti-psychotic treatment breached Article 3
Whether Article 8 required greater weight to be given to autonomy and bodily integrity
Whether Article 14 discrimination arose compared with a capacitated non-detained patient
Whether the SOAD certificate was valid and current
